title: The Sacred Heart at home
hook: families place an image of the Sacred Heart in the home

segments.voice: Yesterday, First Fridays: communion in reparation, nine months running, a promise attached. Your line was nine fridays.

"Behold, I stand at the gate, and knock." That's Christ speaking in the Bible's last book, the one the Douay-Rheims calls the Apocalypse, and the next line says what happens if someone opens. Some Catholic families take that line almost literally. They hang a picture where the family actually lives and invite him in, on purpose, with a small ceremony.
screen: `I STAND AT THE GATE, AND KNOCK.` → `A PICTURE ON THE WALL.` → `AN INVITATION, ON PURPOSE.`

segments.voice: The practice has a formal name: enthronement. A family chooses a picture or statue of the Sacred Heart, Jesus pointing to his heart, and gives it a place of honor: the living room, the kitchen wall, above the table. Not a closet, not a hallway nobody uses. It's meant to be seen in the ordinary traffic of family life. A priest may come to bless the image. The family gathers, prays together, and consecrates the household to the Sacred Heart: a promise to treat Christ as the head of the home. Some families sign a certificate, hang it nearby, and renew the consecration each year on the feast. Tradition links all this to Margaret Mary, who wrote that Jesus promised to bless the places where an image of his heart is set up and honored. The full verse, in the Douay-Rheims: "Behold, I stand at the gate, and knock. If any man shall hear my voice, and open to me the door, I will come in to him, and will sup with him, and he with me." To sup is to eat supper. So the picture isn't decoration, and it isn't a guard dog. It's a reminder that a guest has been invited to the table: to the arguments, the homework, the overdue bills, the birthday cake. Last, what it asks of the household. Hanging an image is easy. Living under it is harder. The hope is that the picture works quietly over time: a sharp word swallowed because he's looking; a short grace before a meal that used to be eaten standing at the counter. One glance at the wall says it: he lives here.
screen: `AN IMAGE IN A PLACE OF HONOR.` · `BLESSED, AND THE HOME CONSECRATED.` · `I WILL COME IN AND SUP WITH HIM.` · `LIVING UNDER IT IS HARDER.` · then, large: `HE LIVES HERE.`

segments.voice: If there's a Sacred Heart picture or any holy image in your home, stand before it, or bring it to mind, and look at it as if for the first time. If you pray, make the sign of the cross toward it and ask God to bless everyone who walks past it. If there's no image, think about where one would go: the room where your household really lives, not the room that's tidy.
The Sacred Heart at home. An image of Christ's heart honored where a family lives, with the household consecrated to him: a standing invitation to a guest at the table.
screen: `THE SACRED HEART AT HOME — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: he lives here. A guest for arguments and birthday cake alike. That's day one thousand three hundred seventy-six.

howItsDone: Some Catholic families enthrone an image of the Sacred Heart in a central room of the house, usually with a blessing by a priest and a family act of consecration, and renew it on the feast of the Sacred Heart.

chat.says: Why does your family have that big picture of Jesus pointing to his heart in the kitchen?
options: It's the Sacred Heart, set where we really live: a sign that Christ is a welcome guest at our table.
It's just art. Catholic homes hang it for decoration, with no prayer or meaning behind it.
It's required. Every Catholic household must enthrone the Sacred Heart to stay in the Church.
chat.meaning: In an enthronement, a family gives an image of the Sacred Heart a place of honor and consecrates the home: a standing invitation, I will sup with him.

notes: The promise to bless places where an image of the Sacred Heart is set up and honored is one of the promises traditionally drawn from Margaret Mary's writings; attributed with 'tradition links' and 'she wrote'. Confirm.

Enthronement details (priest's blessing, family act of consecration, certificate, annual renewal on the feast) are given with 'may' and 'some'; confirm they fairly describe current practice. The movement's promoter (Fr. Mateo Crawley-Boevey) is not named.

The practice invites a lay person to make the sign of the cross toward the image and ask God's blessing on the household; it does not present this as a liturgical blessing of the object. Confirm this is suitable for 'bless your home's image'.
Original: 'Cor Iesu' opening the litany's invocations (e.g. Cor Iesu, Filii Patris aeterni, miserere nobis); confirm ecclesiastical pronunciation.
Editor pass: 'near the end of the Bible' corrected to 'the Bible's last book' (Apocalypse 3 is not near the end); varied the practice's settling line.
